note:
OPERATOR NOTE: `held` MEANS TWO DIFFERENT THINGS AND THE QUEUE WATCHER CANNOT TELL THEM APART. Learned by causing it, just now.

The row states are queued|running|held|landed|reported|superseded|dropped. There is no state for "an operator looked at this and decided not to run it yet", so a deliberate hold has to borrow `held` — which otherwise means "a chamber run stopped, or the mouth refused". I marked two rows held on purpose tonight (one campaign's merge pending their reply, and my own candidate self-deferred behind it), and scripts/queue-watch.sh immediately reported both as:

  QUEUE RED: ... is HELD — needs attribution

They are not reds. Nothing failed, no phase ran, the box was never taken. The watcher is behaving correctly on the information it has; `held` simply carries no distinction between "stopped by a failure" and "stopped by a decision".

WHY MARK THEM AT ALL, rather than just not draining. Because the row is what another operator reads. Leaving a candidate `queued` while privately intending not to run it is a lie in the shared state — the next person to run `sluice-drain.sh` picks it up in FIFO and runs the thing I was deliberately holding, and nothing anywhere would have told them. A false red is a much cheaper failure than an invisible hold, so this is the right trade even though it is noisy.

BOTH ROWS CARRY A NOTE giving the reason, which is where the distinction actually lives:

  set-state <id> held "<why>"

So the recovery for a reader is: a `held` row with an operator note explaining a decision is not a red to attribute; a `held` row whose note names a phase and an rc is. Read the note before chasing the state.

IF THIS RECURS ENOUGH TO BE WORTH FIXING, the shape is a distinct state (`deferred`) rather than teaching the watcher to parse notes — the state is what every consumer keys on, and note-parsing would make the watcher's correctness depend on prose. Not doing that tonight on one occurrence; recording it so a second occurrence is recognised as a pattern rather than rediscovered.
